title: Peh

segments.voice: Yesterday, ayin, the eye, and Hagar by the spring. Your line: ayin is an eye. Today, the letter right after the eye: the mouth.

Moses stands at the burning bush with one more objection, and this one is about his mouth. He tells God he has never been a man of words; he is slow of speech and slow of tongue. A toast, a phone call, a hard conversation: the excuse has a familiar shape. God answers with a question, who made a person's mouth, and then a promise: I will be with your mouth, and teach you what to say. The man whose words fill so much of the Torah starts out afraid to open his.

segments.voice: Peh means a mouth, and the letter makes a p or an f, the sounds your lips make. Four ways to open it. First, the shape. A printed peh can look like a mouth, curved open, with a small mark tucked inside. Some teachers say it's a tongue, waiting. Others say it's a reminder that a mouth holds something back as well as letting it out. Second, Moses. He thinks his mouth disqualifies him. God doesn't argue that he speaks well. God says the mouth was made, and help will come into it. Third, prayer. The Amidah, the standing prayer, is opened with a short line from the Psalms. In the King James words: "O Lord, open thou my lips; and my mouth shall shew forth thy praise." The Talmud discusses saying it there. Before the prayer's own words begin, a person asks for help just to open their mouth. Fourth, the guard. Another psalm asks God to set a watch before the mouth and keep the door of the lips. Jewish ethics has a whole body of law about speech, lashon hara, the evil tongue, warning against harmful talk about others even when it's true. So the mouth here is a door. It opens for praise, teaching and comfort, and it has a doorkeeper. The same peh that can bless can wound, and the tradition takes both seriously. Moses's slow mouth ended up carrying words people still read aloud.
screen: `PEH: A MOUTH, WITH SOMETHING INSIDE.` · `MOSES: SLOW OF SPEECH.` · `OPEN MY LIPS BEFORE THE AMIDAH.` · `A DOOR, AND A DOORKEEPER.` · then, large: `O LORD, OPEN THOU MY LIPS.`

segments.voice: Close your mouth gently and breathe through your nose for a few breaths, noticing how rarely your mouth rests. Then bring to mind one person who would be glad to hear something kind from you, and find the words: true, small and specific, not you're great, but the way you handled that meeting was brave. If you pray, you can ask for help opening your lips.
Peh. A mouth: the letter of the lips, of Moses's slow speech, and of the line said before the Amidah. Today's word.
Your line: peh is a mouth. The same door can bless or wound. Same time tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jews open the Amidah, the central standing prayer, with the verse from Psalm 51 asking God to open their lips; Jewish law on speech, lashon hara, guards against harmful talk about others.

chat.says: Isn't it fine to repeat something bad about someone, as long as it's true?
options: That's lashon hara, the evil tongue: harmful talk about others is warned against even when true.
Yes, Jewish law only forbids lies, so true things can always be passed along freely.
Lashon hara only means cursing; ordinary gossip doesn't count if you stay polite.
